summary: Defines text/enriched, a MIME content type for simple formatted text such as bold and italics. It refines the earlier text/richtext type from RFC 1341. It was replaced by RFC 1563, RFC 1896.

plainLanguage.summary: Plain text is like writing with one pen. This memo lets you add bold and slanted words that show up on any computer.

questions: how to send bold text in email
subtitle: A simple format for sending formatted text in emails.

tldr.problem: Plain text emails are boring, but trying to send rich formatted text across many different email systems is complicated and often fails to display correctly.
tldr.mechanism: text/enriched defines a simple syntax using angle brackets around formatting commands like bold and italic that almost any email system can understand and safely strip if needed.
tldr.outcome: Email systems that understand text/enriched can display bold, italic, and other formatting while systems that do not can still read the message as plain text.

facts.label: Character sets
facts.value: US-ASCII by default; other character sets via charset parameter

today: RFC 1523 is obsoleted by RFC 1563 and RFC 1896. It is no longer the standard definition of text/enriched, though the format remains understood by many email systems. Later MIME content types built on the principles established here.

sections.title: What is text/enriched
sections.content:
RFC 1523 defines text/enriched, a MIME content type that lets email authors add simple formatting to their messages. It refines an earlier format called text/richtext and was designed to work across a wide variety of email systems.

The core idea is to keep formatting simple so that any mail system, even old text-only systems, can strip away the formatting commands and still display readable text. This means formatted email becomes reliable and widely supported instead of fragile and unpredictable.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a special way to mark text in emails so that some computers show it bold or slanted, but all computers can still read the words even if they do not understand the formatting.

sections.title: How text/enriched Works
sections.content:
The syntax is extremely simple. All text represents itself except for the less-than sign < which marks the beginning of a formatting command. Commands are surrounded by angle brackets and are case-insensitive: <bold>, <BOLD>, and <Bold> all mean the same thing.

To end a formatting command, prefix it with a forward slash: </bold>. Formatting commands must be properly balanced and nested, so <bold><italic>text</italic></bold> is correct, but <bold><italic>text</bold></italic> is not.

A literal less-than sign is written as <<, and line breaks are handled specially: a single line break becomes a space, while multiple consecutive line breaks are preserved. This lets mail systems wrap long lines without breaking the formatting.
sections.plainLanguage: You put instructions in angle brackets, like <bold>this is bold</bold>, and the email knows to make the text between them stand out. If you want a real less-than sign, you write it twice.

sections.title: The Formatting Commands
sections.content:
text/enriched defines several types of formatting commands. Font commands change how text looks: <bold> for bold text, <italic> for slanted text, <fixed> for monospace, <underline> for underlined text, and <bigger> or <smaller> for different sizes.

Justification commands control text alignment: <center> centers text, <flushleft> left-aligns with a ragged right edge, and <flushright> right-aligns with a ragged left edge. These commands force line breaks before and after them.

Indentation commands move the left and right margins: <indent> moves the left margin right, and <indentright> moves the right margin left. These do not force line breaks, allowing indented text to start mid-line.

Miscellaneous commands include <excerpt> to mark quoted text from another message, <verbatim> to display text exactly as written without any interpretation, <nofill> to preserve line breaks without justification, and <param> to hide parameters from the reader. Unrecognized commands are safely ignored, allowing for future extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: The commands let you make text bold, slanted, bigger or smaller, centered or pushed to one side, or indented like a quote. Each command is wrapped in angle brackets and closed with a matching closing command.

sections.title: Building a text/enriched Reader
sections.content:
A minimal text/enriched implementation does very little: it recognizes verbatim sections, converts << to a single <, strips out <param> content, removes all other formatting commands by deleting text between angle brackets, and handles line breaks according to the special rules.

A full implementation interprets all the formatting commands and renders the text accordingly. However, the design encourages simplicity in readers because removing formatting should be just as valid as displaying it. Implementations that receive incorrectly nested formatting are encouraged to handle it reasonably, following the principle of being liberal in what you accept.

The RFC includes a sample C program that demonstrates how easily text/enriched can be stripped to plain text, showing that even simple mailers can support the format.
sections.plainLanguage: An email program that understands text/enriched just removes all the angle bracket commands to show the plain text. A fancier program can use the commands to make the text look pretty with bold and colors.

sections.title: Status and Obsolescence
sections.content:
RFC 1523 was published in September 1993 as an Informational RFC. It has been obsoleted by RFC 1563 and RFC 1896, which supersede it with updated specifications.

Despite being superseded, text/enriched established an important principle: that formatted text in email could be simple, interoperable, and safe. The design philosophy influenced later MIME content types and email formatting standards.
sections.plainLanguage: This specification is no longer the official one, as newer versions came later. But the simple idea of marking up text with angle brackets proved useful and influenced how email formatting works today.
